o: Read hexadecimal digits 0–9 and A–F and explain why hex is used.
Convert between eight-bit binary and hexadecimal in four-bit groups.
Convert a two-digit hexadecimal value to denary using place values.
c: Hexadecimal is base 16, using 0–9 and A–F (10–15). The booklet uses colour code #00FF00 to show a practical use: hex shortens binary for humans; computers still store binary.
One hexadecimal digit represents exactly four binary bits (one nibble).
Split an eight-bit value into two four-bit groups and convert each group to one hex digit.
Multiply each hex digit by its positional value, 16 and 1, then add the results.

102.memoryCue: Booklet: hex is shorter and easier for humans to read — it does not replace binary. One nibble = one hex digit. A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. Example colour #00FF00 means full green.

mastery.task: A colour is stored as #00FF00. Explain the three pairs, then change it to pure red and explain why hex is convenient for this representation.
mastery.hint: Each pair is an eight-bit red, green or blue channel ranging from 00 to FF.
mastery.answer: #00FF00: red 00=0, green FF=255, blue 00=0. Pure red is #FF0000. Six hex symbols compactly represent 24 bits of RGB colour.
